40-016.r: "The rule of the Lord of the world extends from Delhi to Palam" was said of the last Tughlaq ruler Nasiruddin Mahmud; BPSC dropped this Bahadur Shah Zafar question.
40-016.c: BPSC removed the question from evaluation; the explanation is about Nasiruddin Mahmud, not Bahadur Shah Zafar.

40-017.r: First Nawab of Oudh (Awadh) → Saadat Khan, made governor in 1722; nephew Safdarjung followed. Iranis founded Oudh, Turanis founded Hyderabad.

40-018.r: Saadat Khan → founder of independent Awadh under Muhammad Shah; sided with Muhammad Shah in the plot against the Sayyid Brothers, so got title Burhan-ul-Mulk. Both statements correct.

40-019.r: Independent Hyderabad → Chin Qilich Khan (Nizam-ul-Mulk), 1724, after Mughal governor Mubarij Khan died in the battle of Sakhar-Kherda.
40-019.t: Don't confuse Chin Qilich Khan (Hyderabad) with Saadat Khan (Awadh).

40-020.r: Qilich Khan = Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah, not Mubariz Khan; he defeated and killed Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda (1724); title Asaf-Jah given by Muhammad Shah, not Zulfiqar Khan.
40-020.c: Answer not printed; the explanation makes (i) and (iii) false, i.e. option (b).

40-021.r: Mysore kingdom (Wodeyars) emerged from vassals of Vijayanagara → correct. Arcot Nizamat was set up by Aurangzeb, not out of Hyderabad; Rohilkhand was formed by Ali Muhammad Khan.

40-022.r: Jantar Mantar, Delhi → Sawai Jai Singh II, Kachhwaha Rajput of Amber; he also built observatories at Ujjain, Mathura, Varanasi and Jaipur.
40-022.h: Jai Singh's five: Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura, Varanasi - "DJ UMV".

40-024.r: Zij (Jiz) Muhammad Shahi, astronomical tables → Sawai Jai Singh II of Jaipur; his observatories: Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura, Varanasi - not Allahabad.
40-024.t: No Jai Singh observatory at Allahabad - a frequent wrong option.

41-001.r: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut on 20 May 1498; welcomed by the Zamorin, the hereditary title of Calicut's rulers.

41-002.r: Vasco da Gama, 1498: Zamorin ruled Calicut; stayed about three months (not a year); came again 1502 and 1524 (not 1501). First Viceroy, Blue Water Policy → Almeida.
hi: Blue Water Policy (नीले पानी की नीति)

41-007.r: Peter Mundy → British traveller (17th century, Shah Jahan's time), not Portuguese; Duarte Barbosa, Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz were Portuguese.

41-008.r: Vasco da Gama → Portugal; Christopher Columbus → Spain; Captain Cook → Great Britain; Tasman → Holland.

41-009.r: Albuquerque → took Goa 1510; Nuno da Cunha → shifted Portuguese HQ from Cochin to Goa; Cabral → reached India Sept 1500; Almeida → Blue Water Policy.

41-010.r: Birthplaces: Christopher Columbus → Italy; Jacques Cartier → France; Sir Francis Drake → UK; Ferdinand Magellan → Portugal.
41-010.t: Columbus sailed for Spain but was born in Italy.

41-011.r: First Europeans to trade with India → Portuguese (Vasco da Gama, Calicut, 1498). Order of arrival: Portuguese, Dutch, English, Danes, French.
41-011.h: "Please Do Enter Dear Friend" = Portuguese, Dutch, English, Danes, French.

41-012.r: Real founder of Portuguese power in India → Albuquerque (1509-15); his first big success: took Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur, Nov 1510.

41-013.r: Wrong statement: Portuguese took Goa in 1499 → actually 1510, by Albuquerque from Bijapur. True: English factories Masulipatnam (south), Orissa 1633 (east); Dupleix took Madras 1746.

41-014.r: First Portuguese fortress in India → Cochin, 1503 (Albuquerque); Almeida built forts at Cannanore and Anjediva in 1505.

41-015.r: First Europeans to set up sea trade centres → Portuguese; Viceroy Almeida won the battle of Diu (1509) over Egypt's Mamluks and Gujarat.

41-016.r: Portuguese in Bengal → Bandel and Hooghly; Hooghly settlement founded 1579 with Akbar's permission.

41-017.r: Pondicherry: first Portuguese, then Dutch (not French second); French dominance from 1673; English held it in 1793, returned it in 1814 (Treaty of Paris). Only statement 1 true.

41-018.r: Hooghly used as a pirate base in the Bay of Bengal → Portuguese; crushed in 1632 by Qasim Khan, Shah Jahan's governor of Bengal.

41-020.r: Founder of Calcutta → Job Charnock, chief of the Qasim Bazar factory; he chose Sutanuti instead of Hooghly.

41-022.r: First Municipal Corporation in India → Madras, 29 Sept 1688; now Greater Chennai Corporation.

41-023.r: First joint-stock company for India trade → English EIC (London, 1600); Dutch EIC next (1602). With English absent from options, answer = Dutch.

41-024.r: Dutch defeated the Portuguese and took Cochin (Kochi) about 1663; in 1714 built Chettuva Fort, called 'Fort William' (Thrissur, Kerala).
41-024.c: The book finds no option fully correct: the Dutch did take Kochi from the Portuguese (about 1663), but their 'Fort William' (1714) stood at Chettuva in Thrissur, not in Kochi.

41-025.r: Correct: Albuquerque took Goa from Bijapur (1510); English Madras factory on land leased from a Vijayanagara representative. Wrong: Dutch first factory Masulipatnam (1605) came after Gajapati decline.

41-026.r: EIC success → all three: no nationalism in India, western-trained army with modern arms, and Indian soldiers serving whoever paid. Royal charter by Elizabeth I, Dec 1600.

41-027.r: First British charter covering India trade → Levant Company (1592, Ottoman trade); EIC later got a 15-year monopoly east of the Cape of Good Hope.
41-027.t: Don't pick East India Company; the Levant Company's charter came first.

41-028.r: English East India Company founded in London in 1600 (charter of Elizabeth I) → Akbar was Mughal emperor (1556-1605).

41-029.r: First English factory → Jahangir's reign: Masulipatnam 1611 (temporary); first permanent factory Surat 1613.
41-029.h: Jahangir = first English factory; Akbar = EIC founded in London.

41-030.r: Battle of Swally (near Surat), 1612 → Captain Thomas Best defeated the Portuguese navy.

41-031.r: First English factory, 1613 → Surat. Steps: Hawkins came 1608, at Mughal court 1609; Middleton got trade permission 1611; Best won at Swally 1612.

41-033.r: Captain William Hawkins reached Surat in 1608 (not 1611) on the ship Hector; at Jahangir's court, Agra, April 1609 with James I's letter; he knew Turkish well.

41-034.r: EIC factories by 1619 → Surat (1613), Agra, Ahmedabad, Baroda, Broach; also Masulipatnam (1611), Armagaon (1628). Not Chicacole or Trichinopoly.

41-035.r: First European company factory at Surat → English, 1613 (Jahangir's permission); Dutch 1616; French 1668.

41-037.r: Early western Presidency of the East India Company → Surat; later shifted to Bombay.

41-038.r: Bombay → from the Portuguese as dowry when Charles II married Catherine of Braganza (treaty 1661); Charles II leased it to EIC in 1668 at 10 pounds a year.

41-039.r: Fort of Prayagraj (Allahabad) handed to the British by Nawab Saadat Ali Khan II of Awadh in 1798.
41-039.c: Answer not printed; explanation's 1798 matches none of the four options.

41-040.r: English governor humbled by Aurangzeb → Sir John Child (Bombay); his 1688 blockade led Aurangzeb to send Sidi Yakub to besiege Bombay.

41-041.r: First Carnatic War (1746-48), English vs French → immediate cause: British capture of French ships; background: Austrian War of Succession in Europe.
41-041.t: Austrian War of Succession is the background, not the immediate cause.

41-043.r: First Carnatic War → ended by Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle; Second → inconclusive; Third → ended by Treaty of Paris; First Mysore War → British lost.

41-044.r: Second Carnatic War → 1749-54 (not 1750-52). First 1746-48; Third 1758-63; Third Battle of Panipat 1761.

41-045.r: Battle of Ambur → 1749 (not 1752); first big battle of Second Carnatic War: Muzaffar Jang, Chanda Sahib and French defeated and killed Anwar-ud-din.

41-046.r: First European to join quarrels of Indian princes to gain territory → Dupleix (French); the English later copied his method.

41-047.r: French East India Company → 1664, by Colbert under Louis XIV; first French factory → Surat (Francois Caron's expedition, 1667).

41-049.r: Founder of the French East India Company → Colbert (1664), finance minister of Louis XIV.

41-050.r: Dutch factory in Bengal → Chinsurah (trade from 1653, proper factory 1656-57); first Dutch post in Bengal at Pipli (1627).

41-051.r: Dutch factories: Bimlipatam → 1641; Karaikal → 1645; Chinsura → 1653; Cochin → 1663.

41-052.r: French failed in the Deccan → English strength, above all the strong British navy; French navy was ruined in the Austrian Succession war (Voltaire).

41-053.r: Order of European entry → Portuguese, Dutch, English, (Danes), French.

41-054.r: Pondicherry → French; Goa → Portuguese; Tranquebar → Danish; Sadras → Dutch.

41-055.r: Europeans got the best shora (saltpetre) and opium from Bihar.

41-056.r: Region famous for opium under British rule → Bihar.

41-057.r: India-China-England triangular trade rested on opium: EIC monopoly on opium in Bengal and Bihar, exported to China; profits bought Chinese goods.

41-058.r: Last Europeans to come as traders → French (1667). Order: Portuguese 1498, Dutch 1605, English 1608, French 1667.

41-059.r: Dutch trade centres → Nagapattinam, Chinsura, Machilipatnam, Surat, Pulicat, Agra, Cochin, Ahmedabad, Patna (all options).

41-060.r: None introduced by the English: land revenue by soil and crop quality → Sher Shah and Akbar; mobile cannons → Mughals; tobacco and red chillies → Portuguese.

41-061.r: Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) → ended Austrian War of Succession and First Carnatic War; English got back Madras.

41-063.r: British success over French → naval superiority, huge wealth and manpower from Bengal, and better internal coordination. Both statements correct.

42-001.r: Last Bengal governor appointed by the Mughal emperor → Murshid Quli Khan (by Farrukh Siyar, 1717); successor Shujauddin was only ratified by Muhammad Shah.

42-003.r: Battle of Plassey, 23 June 1757 → began British supremacy; Clive defeated Siraj-ud-daula; traitors Mir Jafar, Yar Latif Khan, Rai Durlabh.

42-006.r: Siraj-ud-daula was defeated by Clive at Plassey, 1757.
42-006.t: Don't pick Buxar; Siraj-ud-daula's defeat was at Plassey.
